passages.t: A listening son, a guarded mouth, and wealth that lasts
passages.happening:
‘A wise son heeds his father’s discipline, but a mocker does not listen to rebuke’ (verse 1). ‘He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin’ (verse 3). ‘The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied’ (verse 4).

Then come sayings about pretending and money. ‘One pretends to be rich, but has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth’ (verse 7). ‘Riches may ransom a man’s life, but a poor man hears no threat’ (verse 8). ‘The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished’ (verse 9). ‘Arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised’ (verse 10).

‘Dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This chapter adds time to the picture. Several sayings are about how things turn out over the years: quick money dwindles and money gathered little by little grows; a good man's legacy reaches his grandchildren. The book is forming a person who thinks in generations.

Verses 2 to 4 play on one Hebrew word, nephesh, which can mean soul, life, desire or appetite. It comes in each verse with a shifting sense: the faithless desire violence, the guarded mouth protects a life, the slacker's appetite is never filled.

Verse 8 has puzzled readers. One likely sense is that wealth brings its own dangers. The rich attract kidnappers, extortion and lawsuits, and must pay to escape them, while the poor man is not worth threatening. Poverty is not praised. Wealth is shown to carry costs.

A small clay oil lamp burned in every home through the night. A lamp going out was a picture of a household coming to an end.
passages.later: The psalm agrees with verse 11 and the slow way: ‘Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked’ (Psalm 37:16).
passages.asks: The chapter values what is built slowly. Ask whether you are chasing something quick that will dwindle. And ask whom you are listening to, since the wise son begins by hearing correction.

passages.t: Hope deferred, and the company you keep
passages.happening:
“Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life” (verse 12).

Then the chapter returns to teaching. ‘The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death’ (verse 14). ‘Good understanding wins favor, but the way of the faithless is difficult’ (verse 15). ‘A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing’ (verse 17). ‘Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored’ (verse 18). ‘Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul’ (verse 19).

‘He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Verse 12 is one of the Bible's most honest lines about longing. It does not tell anyone to stop wanting, or pretend that waiting does not hurt. Delayed hope makes the heart sick. And when a longing is at last fulfilled, it is like a tree of life, the picture of Eden and of a life that flourishes. Verse 19 comes back to the same thought.

There was no postal service. A messenger carried his sender's words, and often his authority. A faithful envoy could mend a situation, and a wicked one could start a war or ruin an agreement.

Verse 20 is about who shapes a person. People become like the company they keep, for good or ill.
passages.later: The psalmist chose his companions this way: ‘I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts’ (Psalm 119:63). And Paul quotes a saying of his own day that agrees with verse 20: “Bad company corrupts good character” (1 Corinthians 15:33).
passages.asks: The chapter admits that waiting can make the heart sick. Ask what hope you are carrying that has been delayed, and bring it honestly to God. And ask who you are walking with most days, and who you are becoming because of it.

passages.t: An inheritance, the poor man's field, and the rod
passages.happening:
‘Disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous’ (verse 21). ‘A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is passed to the righteous’ (verse 22).

Then one of the book's sharpest sayings about the poor: “Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away” (verse 23).

“He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently” (verse 24). ‘A righteous man eats to his heart’s content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
In Israel land was not a thing to be sold for good. It belonged to the LORD and was held by families from one generation to the next (Leviticus 25:23). Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to King Ahab because it was the inheritance of his fathers. To leave an inheritance to grandchildren was to keep the family's place in Israel.

Verse 23 matters for how the whole book is read. The poor man's field could feed his family, but without justice his harvest was swept away: by powerful neighbors, corrupt courts and creditors, not only by drought or laziness. The prophets of the eighth century BC, Amos, Isaiah and Micah, accused Israel's leaders of exactly this. Proverbs agrees with them. Poverty is not always a person's own fault.

The chapter began with a son hearing his father's discipline (verse 1). By verse 24 that son is a father who must correct his own child. Rod is shevet, a word that also names a shepherd's staff and a ruler's scepter. Proverbs uses it of correcting adult fools as well as sons (10:13; 26:3).
passages.later: Isaiah warned those who swallow up the land of the poor: ‘Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land’ (Isaiah 5:8). And Paul gives fathers a limit: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).
passages.hard:
Does verse 24 tell parents to spank their children?

Faithful Christian parents answer this differently, and both answers deserve a fair hearing.

Many read verse 24, with 22:15, 23:13-14 and 29:15, as instruction for parents. For them, measured physical discipline of a young child, given calmly and in love, never in anger and never to injure, takes wrong seriously and is then over. They note that the verse's point is that holding back correction is a failure of love, not a kindness.

Others read the rod as a picture of correction in general. The same book uses the rod of adult fools, which few Christians would apply to adults, and they hold that Proverbs describes the methods of its own culture rather than a technique for every age. They correct through consequences, teaching and close relationship, and they point to the New Testament's word that fathers must not provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21).

This question divides faithful parents without dividing anyone from Christ. These notes take no side.

On what matters most, both agree. The verse assumes a parent who loves the child and aims at the child's good, not a parent letting out anger. Its real target is the parent who never corrects at all, which Proverbs calls a kind of hatred. Correction given in anger, or that injures a child, is not discipline at all. Nothing in this verse gives anyone a warrant to harm a child, and the whole Bible condemns injury and abuse.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The chapter thinks in generations. Ask what you are passing on to those who come after you, in faith as well as in money. And if you are a parent, ask whether your correction comes from love for your child's good, and whether your child knows it.
